extracted.intended_audience: practitioners registered before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), OED/disciplinary counsel, and USPTO adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria the USPTO (and its adjudicators) apply to determine whether a practitioner has violated Rules of Professional Conduct and what sanctions are appropriate, with examples of misconduct (e.g., failing to remit client maintenance fees) and aggravating/mitigating considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.102(a) — Abide by client's decisions concerning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall abide by a client's decisions concerning the objectives of representation and, as required by § 11.104, shall consult with the client as to the means by which they are to be pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to submit filing/maintenance fees remitted by clients or failing to communicate while knowing or having reason to know that patent applications have been abandoned violates §11.102(a). Example: invoicing client for maintenance fees but not remitting them (In re Gibson). Practitioners must follow client directions about maintaining patents and consult on means to pursue the client's objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — Act with reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules require a practitioner to act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence is defined as persevering attention and care required in the situation (Black's; MRPC r.1.3). Personal inconvenience is not a defense though may affect sanctions. Examples of violation: failing to remit maintenance fees before deadlines, ceasing communication with client about pending matters (In re Virga).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a) & (b) — Consult, keep client informed, and explain matters for informed decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: §11.104(a) requires: (1) Promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance requiring informed consent; (2) reasonably consult about means to accomplish objectives; (3) keep the client reasonably informed about status; (4) promptly comply with reasonable requests for information; (5) consult about limitations when client expects impermissible assistance. §11.104(b) requires explaining a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include failing to tell client that maintenance fees were not remitted, not informing client that patents expired, not advising on steps for reinstatement, and not notifying client of termination. See In re Pasquine. Practitioners must provide timely status updates and sufficient explanation for client decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(a) — Hold client property separate from practitioner's property
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must hold client property in connection with the representation separate from the practitioner's own property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Client funds must not be mixed with practitioner funds. Depositing client-provided maintenance fees into an operating account that contains the practitioner's personal funds violates §11.115(a) (see In re Kroll, In re Larson). Maintaining client funds in a personal/operating account is an aggravating misconduct example.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(c) — Deposit advanced legal fees/expenses into client trust account
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall deposit into a client trust account legal fees and expenses that have been paid in advance to be withdrawn by the practitioner only as fees are earned or expenses incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advanced payments labeled as fees or expenses must be kept in trust and withdrawn only as earned. Retaining advance fees in an operating account or withdrawing unearned fees is a violation. This rule corresponds to ABA Model Rule 1.15(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d) — Prompt delivery of funds or property to client or third persons
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall promptly deliver to the client or third person any funds or other property that the client or third person is entitled to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third parties entitled to funds (e.g., USPTO, CIPO) must be paid when due. Failing to remit filing or maintenance fees collected from a client is a §11.115(d) violation (see In re Hamill). Model Rule 1.15 similarly requires prompt delivery to interested third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d) — Duties upon termination to protect client's interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination of representation, a practitioner shall take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client's interests (e.g., providing reasonable notice, allowing time to obtain other counsel, surrendering property, refunding unearned fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners who effectively abandon representation without notice, accounting, refunding unearned fees, or cooperating with successor counsel violate §11.116(d). Examples include failing to notify client of termination and not providing instructions or restitution needed to revive expired patents (see In re Ries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation of any Rule is grounds for discipline — 37 C.F.R. § 11.19
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners registered to practice before the USPTO are subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Office; violation of any Rule of Professional Conduct is grounds for discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any breach of the Rules cited (communication, diligence, safekeeping funds, etc.) can trigger disciplinary proceedings under §11.19. The decision cites this as the statutory basis for sanctioning the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) — Four factors to consider in determining sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining any sanction, consider if applicable: (1) Whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; (4) The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four factors form the required explanation for sanctions. The decision applies them to weigh fiduciary breach, mental state, actual monetary/patent injury, and aggravators (dishonesty, multiple offenses, experience, indifference) vs. mitigators (personal problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.20 — Types of sanctions and reinstatement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon finding grounds for discipline, a respondent may be excluded from practice before the USPTO, suspended for an appropriate period, reprimanded or censured, or placed on probation. Reinstatement may be conditioned on restitution, successful completion of professional responsibility training, or other appropriate measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions range from reprimand to exclusion. Reinstatement is discretionary and may require restitution (the decision orders payment of $8,840), training, or other conditions. The decision imposes a two-year suspension plus two years' probation upon reinstatement and restitution as a condition to reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental-state definitions and relevance (ABA Standards) — intentional vs. knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Intentional’ is acting with a conscious objective or purpose to accomplish a particular result. ‘Knowing’ is acting with conscious awareness of the nature or attendant circumstances of the conduct without the conscious objective to accomplish a particular result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental state affects sanctions: intentionally failing to submit fees or intentionally concealing communications supports harsher discipline. The decision finds the respondent acted intentionally because he invoiced for fees and yet did not remit them and concealed the conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (ABA Standards §§ 9.22, 9.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include dishonest or selfish motive; multiple offenses; substantial experience in the practice of law; indifference to making restitution. Mitigating factors include personal or emotional problems and lack of prior disciplinary record (among others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravators support increased sanctions (examples cited from case law). Mitigators may reduce sanctions but may be outweighed by aggravators and actual harm. The decision lists four aggravators relied upon by OED and acknowledges one mitigating factor (respondent's personal tragedies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiduciary duty to client and duties to public and profession
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner before the USPTO owes a fiduciary duty to clients and duties to the public and the legal profession to comply with the Rules and maintain public confidence in the patent bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaches of fiduciary duties (e.g., failing to remit client funds, not communicating, retaining unearned fees) constitute serious violations because they harm the client and erode public trust in the profession. The decision treats such breaches as central to sanctioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative misconduct patterns that constitute violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific behaviors that the decision identifies as violations include: invoicing clients for filing/maintenance fees but depositing the funds into a practitioner operating account; failing to remit fees to USPTO or foreign offices; ceasing communications with client inquiries; retaining unearned legal fees; failing to notify client of expiration/termination or to cooperate in reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These anti-patterns are repeatedly cited in prior precedents (In re Hamill, In re Larson, In re Kroll, etc.) and are used as concrete examples of §11.102, §11.103, §11.104, §11.115, and §11.116 violations. They also inform the assessment of actual injury and aggravating factors.
